title: What Is a Process
summary: A process is a program in execution — its own address space, registers, and open files. This is the abstraction every OS interview question about concurrency and isolation builds on.

slides.markdown:
A **process** is the OS's answer to a simple problem: many programs want to run on a machine with one (or a few) CPUs, and none of them should be able to read or crash the others by accident.

A process is a program **in execution** — code plus everything the OS tracks to run it in isolation: its own memory, its own view of the CPU's registers, its own table of open files. Every later topic — scheduling, threads, IPC, deadlocks — is really asking questions about this one abstraction.

Think of a process as a sealed room: the program's code runs inside, and nothing leaks in or out unless the OS explicitly builds a door (a pipe, a shared memory segment, a socket).

slides.sectionTitle: Program vs process: code at rest vs code in execution
slides.markdown:
A **program** is a passive file on disk — a binary or script, just bytes sitting in storage. It does nothing until someone runs it.

A **process** is that program loaded into memory and given resources to actually execute: a stack, a heap, registers, a program counter pointing at the next instruction. Run the same program twice and you get two independent processes, each with its own memory and its own PID, even though they started from identical bytes on disk.

This distinction matters in interviews because "program" and "process" get used interchangeably in casual speech, but an OS question like "how many processes does this create" only makes sense once you separate the static file from the running instance.

slides.sectionTitle: What's inside a process: address space, registers, open files
slides.markdown:
Every process the OS creates comes bundled with:

- A **virtual address space** — its own private view of memory, mapped by the OS to physical RAM so it can't see or touch another process's memory.
- **CPU register values** — program counter, stack pointer, and general-purpose registers, saved whenever the process isn't actively running on a core.
- A **table of open file descriptors** — every file, socket, or pipe the process has open, indexed by small integers (0, 1, 2 are stdin/stdout/stderr by convention).
- Metadata the OS needs to manage it: process ID, owner, priority, and scheduling state.

All of this together is what the OS calls the process's **context** — everything needed to pause it and resume it later as if nothing happened.

![Process address space layout](assets/process-address-space.svg)

A process's address space is laid out in regions. The **text segment** holds the compiled machine instructions (usually read-only, so a bug can't overwrite the program itself). The **data segment** holds global and static variables. The **heap** holds dynamically allocated memory and grows upward as you allocate more. The **stack** holds function call frames — local variables, return addresses — and grows downward from the top of the address space.

The heap and stack grow toward each other from opposite ends specifically so both can expand into the same unused gap without a fixed size limit baked in ahead of time.

slides.sectionTitle: The stack and heap within a process
slides.markdown:
The **stack** is managed automatically: every function call pushes a frame with its local variables and return address, and returning pops it off. It's fast — allocation is just moving a pointer — but fixed in total size, which is why unbounded recursion causes a **stack overflow**.

The **heap** is managed explicitly (`malloc`/`free` in C, `new`/garbage collection in higher-level languages). It's slower to allocate from — the allocator has to find a free block — but it can grow much larger and the memory outlives the function that created it, which is why you heap-allocate anything you need to return or share.

Rule of thumb an interviewer expects: stack for short-lived, function-scoped data; heap for anything that must outlive the function or whose size isn't known at compile time.

Every process gets a unique **PID** (process ID) assigned by the OS at creation, used everywhere to name it — `kill <pid>`, `/proc/<pid>` on Linux, task manager entries.

Every process (except the very first) also has a **PPID** (parent process ID) — the PID of whoever created it. This forms a **process tree**: on Linux, PID 1 (`init` or `systemd`) sits at the root, and every other process traces a chain of parents back to it.

The parent-child relationship matters beyond bookkeeping: it determines who is responsible for reaping a process when it exits (see the fork/exec/wait topic) and who a process gets reparented to if its original parent dies first.

You can see this tree directly on any Unix system:

```bash
ps -ef --forest       # process list with parent/child indentation
pstree -p             # visual tree of PIDs
cat /proc/1234/status # PID 1234's PPID, memory, state — straight from the kernel
```

`ps -ef` shows `UID PID PPID ... CMD` — the PPID column is exactly the parent link from the previous slide. `/proc/<pid>/` on Linux is literally how tools like `ps` and `top` get their data: the kernel exposes each process's state as a virtual filesystem, so there's no special API needed to inspect a process from the outside.

Being fluent with `ps`/`pstree` is a small but real interview signal — it shows you've actually operated a Unix system, not just read about processes in a textbook.

A process starts with exactly one **thread of execution** — one program counter, one call stack, one path through the code. That's a **single-threaded** process.

A process can also spawn additional threads that run concurrently within the *same* address space — a **multi-threaded** process. All its threads share the code, data, and heap, but each thread keeps its own stack and registers, because each is independently executing instructions.

This is just a preview: the full trade-off between using more threads versus more processes is its own topic, but the key distinction to hold onto here is that "process" and "thread of execution" aren't the same thing — a process is a container that holds one or more threads.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming two processes share memory by default
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I set a global variable in process A, so process B should see the new value too — they're both part of the same app."

**Why it's wrong:** each process has its own private virtual address space. A global variable lives at some virtual address in process A's memory, mapped to a physical page that process B's page tables simply don't reference. Process B's "same" variable, if it exists at all, is a completely separate copy in its own memory.

**Correct model:** memory isolation between processes is the default and the entire point of the process abstraction — it's what stops one crashing or misbehaving process from corrupting another. Sharing data across processes requires an explicit, OS-provided mechanism (shared memory, a pipe, a socket, a file) — never just "both processes reference the same variable name."

slides.sectionTitle: Why isolation costs something: the staff-level nuance
slides.markdown:
Process isolation isn't free. Every memory access a process makes has to go through **virtual-to-physical address translation** (page tables, backed by a hardware TLB), and every switch between processes typically means flushing or re-tagging that translation cache — one reason process context switches are noticeably more expensive than thread context switches (covered in Context Switching).

This is why some high-performance systems deliberately trade isolation for speed: a single multi-threaded process avoids per-process translation overhead entirely, while a microkernel or sandboxed multi-process design accepts that overhead in exchange for a crash in one component not taking down everything else.

A staff-level answer names this trade-off explicitly instead of treating "more processes" or "more threads" as a free architectural choice.
